title: The Department's policy on the effective date of interchangeability and on midstream interchange
subtopic: Effective date of interchangeability and midstream interchange
rule_summary: The Department of Public Health Drug Control Program's Policy on drug interchangeability and midstream interchange, which sets out procedures in accordance with M.G.L. c. 17, § 13, M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D and 105 CMR 720.000, states that pharmacists must dispense a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product provided that the product is listed in the MLID and the prescriber has not indicated 'no substitution', and that a pharmacist shall interchange accordingly when dispensing a new prescription or a prescription refill presented after the effective date of interchangeability, which the policy defines as not later than 90 days after the date of listing of the drug product in the MLID. It defines the date of listing as the date the Orange Book edition or supplement is postmarked or posted electronically by the United States Department of Health and Human Services, whichever is first, for products listed from the Orange Book under 105 CMR 720.050; the date the Additional List is published by the Secretary of State in the Massachusetts Register, for Additional List products; and the date the Exception List is so published, for products listed under 105 CMR 720.080. It states that there is no requirement to wait the full 90 days to initiate an interchange. It defines midstream interchange as the first time an interchangeable drug product is dispensed pursuant to a prescription written prior to the date of listing on which the drug changed from sole source to multi-source, and states that a pharmacist presented with a new prescription or prescription refill that requires midstream interchange shall notify the patient and prescriber of that requirement in those cases in which such notification is, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, reasonably indicated for the proper care of the patient; that the notification may be written or oral and may be conveyed by telephone, facsimile, electronic transmission or other approved means; that once notification is provided there is no requirement for an acknowledgment or response from the patient or prescriber; that to prevent a midstream interchange the prescriber must issue a new prescription that indicates 'no substitution', which a prescriber may do at any time; and that a copy of the notification or a notation that it was provided should be maintained in the pharmacy record.
exam_relevance: Tests the Department's position that interchange of a newly listed product becomes required no later than 90 days after listing and may begin sooner, that notice of a midstream interchange turns on the pharmacist's professional judgment and needs no acknowledgment, and that a new prescription indicating 'no substitution' is what prevents the interchange.

authority.section: Policy part I (definitions), part II (drug interchangeability), part III (midstream interchange) and summary

numeric_facts.fact: Latest effective date of interchangeability, as the Department's policy states it
numeric_facts.conditions: Not later than 90 days after the date of listing in the MLID; the policy states there is no requirement to wait the full 90 days

exceptions: Notification of a midstream interchange is called for in those cases in which it is, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, reasonably indicated for the proper care of the patient.
common_confusions: Treating the 90 days as a waiting period. The policy states there is no requirement to wait the full 90 days to initiate an interchange.

Waiting for the patient's or prescriber's response to a midstream notice. The policy states that no acknowledgment or response is required; a new prescription indicating 'no substitution' is what prevents the interchange.
Reading the policy's statement that a copy or notation of the notification should be maintained as a regulatory mandate. It is Department guidance phrased as 'should'.
verification_notes: Read in the Department of Public Health Drug Control Program policy page published on mass.gov on 2026-09-16; the page is linked from the Department's Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs page.
